Research Interests

Moving information with light, classical and quantum.

Quantum light sources

Photon pairs · squeezed light
The 3D view needs WebGL, which this browser has turned off.

In a high-Q Si₃N₄ microring, a χ⁽³⁾ material, two pump photons can annihilate and create a signal–idler pair on neighboring resonances (spontaneous four-wave mixing). In a periodically poled lithium niobate waveguide, a χ⁽²⁾ material, one pump photon at twice the frequency splits into a pair (spontaneous parametric down-conversion), and the poling period Λ sets the phase matching. In both, detecting one photon heralds the other.

Driven harder, the same nonlinear processes produce squeezed light: one quadrature's noise falls below the vacuum level. How far below depends on loss, so source purity and low-loss design decide what is usable.

Quantum frequency conversion

Quantum interconnect
Converter · memory photon to telecom
The 3D view needs WebGL, which this browser has turned off.

Most quantum memories emit photons at visible or near-infrared wavelengths, where optical fiber is lossy. Quantum frequency conversion shifts a single photon to a telecom wavelength while keeping its quantum state, so it can travel kilometers of fiber.

A strong pump and a χ⁽²⁾ waveguide carry out the shift through difference-frequency generation. The practical targets are high conversion efficiency and low added noise from the pump, both set by the waveguide design.

Optical interconnects & co-packaged optics

Classical links
Link · co-packaged optics, 4 channels
The 3D view needs WebGL, which this browser has turned off.

One comb source supplies many evenly spaced wavelengths on a single fiber. In the scene above, four of them link two co-packaged modules: each ring modulator writes data onto its own color, and at the receiver a matching ring filter drops that color into its own photodetector.

Packaging these photonic chiplets next to the driver and receiver electronics keeps the electrical path short, which is what sets energy per bit in chip-to-chip and memory links.

On-Chip Quantum Frequency Conversion in TFLN-on-SiN Waveguides

Seoul National University (SNU), Q-SPIN Lab, Republic of Korea
Project with Samsung Advanced Institute of Technology (SAIT)
780 nm → 1300 nm⁸⁷Rb photon to telecom O-band
  • Designed an on-chip quantum frequency conversion (QFC) device that shifts 780 nm single photons from ⁸⁷Rb atoms to the 1300 nm telecom band by difference-frequency generation with a 1950 nm pump, so the photons can travel through low-loss optical fiber. The photon and the pump are combined in a fiber WDM before the chip and the leftover pump is filtered after it, so the chip itself needs only one straight waveguide. Both designs below use the same platform, a thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) film that is bonded on a Si₃N₄ strip waveguide and left unetched. They differ in how the three waves are phase-matched.

WavelengthsWhy a 1950 nm pump

Noise · 1570 nm pump
Noise · 1950 nm pump

Schematic spectra (axis not to scale).

  • Both approaches convert 780 nm to 1300 nm with a 1950 nm pump. This puts the 1300 nm output 650 nm away from the pump, outside its Raman band. With a 1570 nm pump the 1550 nm output would lie only 20 nm from the pump, inside the band.
  • A short, efficient converter also needs less pump power, which lowers the remaining SHG–SPDC noise.

Approach 1Modal phase matching with laterally split-poled domains

350 %/W/cm²simulated normalized efficiency
Device · laterally split-poled TFLN on a buried SiN strip
Principle · laterally split-poled domains

Mode profiles from Lumerical MODE (outlines of the LN film and the SiN strip added).

  • Light is guided by a Si₃N₄ strip under a bonded z-cut thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) layer. Modal phase matching places the 780 nm light in the TM10 mode and the 1300 nm and 1950 nm light in TM00, so momentum is conserved without periodic poling.
  • Because TM10 is odd across the waveguide, a uniform χ⁽²⁾ makes the nonlinear overlap cancel. Laterally split-poled domains, two LN domains of opposite sign split at the waveguide center, make the integrand even, so both lobes add and the coupling κ becomes nonzero.
  • The internal conversion efficiency follows , so the design raises through the mode overlap while keeping the propagation loss low.

Approach 2Quasi-phase matching with periodic poling

10,390 %/W/cm²simulated normalized efficiency2.8 mmfull-conversion length at 310 mW
Device · periodically poled TFLN on a buried SiN strip
aSimulated mode profiles
bCalculated internal efficiency against device length

The cutaway is schematic and not to scale. (a) Mode profiles from Lumerical MODE (outlines of the LN film and the SiN strip added). (b) Calculated for three 780 nm losses, with a 1300 nm loss of 0.1 dB/cm and an undepleted pump.

  • The LN film is x-cut and periodically poled. All three waves travel in the fundamental TE00 mode with the field along the crystal z axis, so the interaction uses d33 (type-0). Reversing the sign of d33 every coherence length keeps the converted field growing.
  • Mode simulations (Ansys Lumerical MODE) give a normalized efficiency of about 10,390 %/W/cm², about 30 times that of Approach 1.
  • At a pump power of 310 mW the full-conversion length is 2.8 mm. A converter this short tolerates propagation loss: for an assumed 780 nm loss of 0.5–1.6 dB/cm, the calculated peak internal efficiency is 95–98 %.
  • The LN film is bonded and poled but never etched, and the waveguide is a foundry Si₃N₄ strip. The 780 nm loss is an assumed range and poling errors are not included. The next steps are to measure the 780 nm loss, pole the bonded film, and measure DFG.

Linewidth engineering

Refs: Z. Vernon et al., Opt. Lett. 42, 3638 (2017) · Y. Liu et al., Opt. Lett. 45, 73 (2020)

  • Two asymmetric MZI couplers with a path difference of πR address alternate ring resonances, so the pump linewidth (low Q) and the signal/idler linewidths (high Q) are set independently.

The 3D view needs WebGL, which this browser has turned off.
Coupling engineering

Ref: X. Jia et al., Nat. Photon. 20, 428 (2026)

  • Two asymmetric MZIs with twice the ring FSR address alternate resonances: MZI 1 critically couples the pump in, while MZI 2 strongly over-couples the signal and idler out to the drop port; the escape efficiency reaches 0.975 while the pump threshold rises only linearly.
  • An auxiliary ring (FSR ratio 3:4 with the principal ring) hybridizes with the idler resonance, so squeezers across a 6-inch Si3N4 wafer can be spectrally aligned; Jia et al. measured −2.7 dB single-mode and −3.3 dB two-mode squeezing, or −7.5 dB and −9.7 dB inferred on chip.

Ring resonators and critical coupling

Introduction: what is a ring resonator

A ring resonator is a waveguide closed into a loop and placed next to a straight bus waveguide. Light in the bus can cross the small gap into the ring, but it only builds up there at certain wavelengths, the resonances, where the light comes back in step with itself after every round trip.

Physical meaning of critical coupling

Send a laser into the bus waveguide and measure the power at the other end with a photodetector.

Critical coupling means that the input light is ‘critically coupled’ to the ring resonator, resulting in zero output intensity at the output port.

Physical intuition of critical coupling

Two fields meet at the output. is the part of the input that stays in the bus. is light that has gone around the ring and couples back into the bus. On resonance the two arrive exactly out of phase, so what leaves the chip is their difference.

As the bus–ring gap decreases,

  • Weak coupling. Little light crosses the gap, is much smaller than , and .
  • Near critical. grows and the dip gets deeper.
  • Critical coupling. The two fields have the same size and cancel completely: .
  • Overcoupling. is now the larger of the two, so again.

Mach–Zehnder interferometers: MZI and AMZI

Introduction: what is an MZI

A Mach–Zehnder interferometer (MZI) is two directional couplers (DC) joined by two waveguide arms. The first coupler splits the incoming light between the arms, the arms carry the two parts separately, and the second coupler brings them back together. Which output the light leaves from is decided by one thing: the phase difference between the two arms when they meet again.

MZI as an interferometer switch

Send light into In 1 only and use 50:50 couplers. Then the phase shifter alone decides where the light goes.

Why does half a period of phase move all the light?

There are two ways to reach each output, one through each arm, and what comes out is their sum. Every time light crosses over inside a coupler its phase shifts by a quarter of a period (this is the factor in the equations below). Going straight through adds nothing.

  • Out 1. The path through the lower arm crosses over twice, : half a period in total. With it arrives exactly opposite to the path through the upper arm, and for 50:50 couplers the two cancel.
  • Out 2. Both paths cross over once, so they arrive in step and add up. All the light is here.
  • Now set . The path through the upper arm is delayed by another half period, so the two paths add at Out 1 and cancel at Out 2. The switch has flipped.
Try it
02π

The phase shifter

A phase shifter delays the light in one arm without changing the arm's length. It changes the effective index of a section of length by . When the index goes up, the wave is slightly shorter inside that section and leaves it delayed by

Two common ways to change the index:

  • Thermo-optic (heater). A metal strip above the waveguide heats it, and the index rises with temperature. It is simple and works in almost any material, but it is slow and draws power for as long as the phase is held.
  • Electro-optic. A voltage across a material such as lithium niobate changes the index directly (the Pockels effect). It is fast and needs almost no power to hold a state, but it needs an electro-optic material.

The drive needed for is the usual figure of merit, for a heater and for an electro-optic shifter: it is exactly what it takes to flip the switch from one output to the other.

AMZI as a wavelength-dependent coupler

Then, can we design a wavelength-dependent switch using this structure?

Yes: make one arm longer than the other by (an asymmetric MZI, AMZI). The longer arm delays the light by , and this depends on the wavelength, because what matters is how many wavelengths fit into .

So one AMZI sends to one output and to the other: a wavelength-dependent coupler. The phase shifter on the long arm is still there to fine-tune which wavelengths go where.

Try it
shortlong

The drawing is not to scale. A real holds many wavelengths, so a much smaller change in wavelength is enough to swap the outputs.

Theory notes

Quantum frequency conversion: how a single photon changes color

Introduction: why change the color of a photon?

Quantum memories such as atoms, ions and color centers emit photons in the visible or near-infrared. Rubidium atoms, for example, emit at 780 nm. Optical fiber is lossy at these wavelengths, so most photons are lost within a few kilometers. Only the telecom bands, around 1300 nm and 1550 nm, can cross tens of kilometers of fiber.

WavelengthFiber lossSurvives 10 kmSurvives 50 km
780 nmabout 4 dB/km0.01%10−20
1300 nmabout 0.35 dB/km45%1.8%
1550 nmabout 0.2 dB/km63%10%

Fraction of photons that survive: , where is the total loss in dB (loss per kilometer × length). Typical values for single-mode fiber.

So to connect two distant quantum nodes, the photon has to be moved to a telecom wavelength before it enters the fiber. Everything that makes it quantum has to stay untouched: it must remain a single photon, keep its coherence, and stay entangled with the memory it came from. Changing the color of a photon while keeping its quantum state is called quantum frequency conversion (QFC).

This note uses one example throughout: a 780 nm signal photon is converted to a 1300 nm target photon with a 1950 nm pump laser.

Physical intuition

How can a photon change color?

A photon cannot change its energy by itself. In a material with a second-order nonlinearity , three light fields can exchange photons with each other, and the energy always balances:

Here s is the signal (780 nm), t is the target (1300 nm) and p is the pump (1950 nm). One signal photon carries exactly the energy of one target photon plus one pump photon.

What does the pump do?

The pump is a strong laser at the third color. It drives the exchange: the stronger the pump field, the faster signal photons turn into target photons. The pump holds an enormous number of photons, so gaining or losing one changes nothing for it. It behaves as a fixed classical field whose only role is to set how strongly the two other colors are coupled.

What remains is a swap between two colors. One signal photon disappears and one target photon appears, or the reverse. The total number of signal and target photons never changes, and no photon is created from nothing. This is why the conversion can be free of added noise.

A beam splitter between two colors

A beam splitter mixes two beams: a photon that arrives in one beam leaves in a superposition of the two. The pumped waveguide does the same to two colors that travel in the same waveguide. As the photon moves along, its probability flows from the signal color to the target color as , where is the coupling strength set by the pump. At the photon is entirely at the target color. If the waveguide goes on, the photon starts to come back.

Try it
0π

The three-wave Hamiltonian

Each of the three fields has an annihilation part and a creation part. removes one photon from the mode and adds one:

The interaction energy of a material is proportional to the product of the three fields,

so it contains 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 terms, and each term rotates at its own frequency. With they form four pairs, a term and its Hermitian conjugate:

TermConjugateRotates atResult
Kept
Averages to zero
Averages to zero
Averages to zero

Terms that rotate at optical frequencies average to zero over any time we can measure (the rotating-wave approximation). Only the pair that conserves energy remains:

The second term (DFG) removes a signal photon and adds a target photon and a pump photon: the down-conversion in the picture above. The first term (SFG) is its reverse. They always come together, because must be Hermitian. The strength is set by and by how well the three modes overlap inside the waveguide.

A strong pump turns it into a two-color swap

The pump is a laser in a coherent state with a mean photon number . Its relative fluctuation is , which is negligible for a bright beam: 100 mW at 1950 nm is about 1018 photons per second. Converting signal photons one at a time does not deplete it either. So the pump operator can be replaced by a number (the undepleted-pump approximation):

The pump phase only fixes the phase reference of the target mode, so it can be absorbed into the definition of that mode. The result is

This is the beam-splitter Hamiltonian. It removes a photon from one color and adds it to the other, and its strength is a knob: it grows with the square root of the pump power.

Why no noise is added: it depends on which field is the strong one. Call the three frequencies . The same interaction gives two different machines.

Strong field at a lower frequency,

A swap. Each term removes one photon and adds one, so the total number of photons never changes.

Vacuum in, vacuum out. Nothing is added: this is frequency conversion (1 is the signal, 2 the target, 3 the pump).

Strong field at the highest frequency,

Pair creation. One pump photon splits into two photons that appear together.

Photons appear even with nothing at the input. This makes photon pairs and squeezed light, and it would be noise in a converter.

From the Hamiltonian to an oscillation

The operators evolve by the Heisenberg equation of motion,

With the commutator is , and likewise for the other mode. This gives two coupled equations,

Differentiating once more decouples them into the equation of a harmonic oscillator,

whose solution is

In a waveguide the interaction time is the time the photon has spent inside, , where is the group velocity. From here on we write , with counted per unit length:

The matrix is unitary, so is the same at every : no photon is lost and none is added.

The same matrix as a beam splitter

A beam splitter transforms its two input modes as

Here is a mixing angle, not a geometric one: is the transmission amplitude and the reflection amplitude, so is a 50:50 splitter. The waveguide matrix has the same form with . The factor is only a phase convention: writing the target mode as gives exactly the matrix above. It is also the directional coupler of the MZI note, with through coefficient and cross coefficient . The crossing factor written there plays the role of here.

One photon in

Send in one signal photon and nothing at the target color, . The Hamiltonian connects this state only with ,

so the photon stays within these two states:

The photon is in a superposition of two colors. The probabilities of finding it at each color are

Three lengths to remember
50:50, an equal superposition of the two colors
Full conversion
Back at the signal color

Why the quantum state survives. At the operator solution reads : the target mode at the output is the signal mode at the input, up to a fixed phase. This is a statement about the operator, so it holds for any input state. A single photon stays a single photon, and a photon that was entangled with a memory is still entangled with it after the conversion. Because has no pair-creation term, no extra photons are added on the way.

Design rule: stop at the first peak

A longer waveguide sends the photon back toward the signal color. In practice is written with the normalized efficiency of the waveguide, in %/(W·cm²), and the pump power :

Length and pump power trade against each other: doubling the length cuts the pump power for full conversion by four. For example, a waveguide with 1000 %/(W·cm²) and a length of 1 cm needs about 250 mW.

What this ideal picture leaves out

  • Phase matching. Everything above assumes that momentum is conserved as well as energy, . With a mismatch the conversion never reaches 1. That is the subject of a separate note.
  • Loss. Propagation and coupling loss remove photons. With the same loss coefficient (per unit length) at both colors, .
  • Noise. The swap adds no photons, but the strong pump can create unwanted ones through spontaneous Raman scattering and parametric fluorescence. This is why the pump is placed far from the target wavelength and the output is filtered narrowly.

Theory notes

Lithium niobate as a χ⁽²⁾ material: x-cut and z-cut

Introduction: one axis decides everything

Lithium niobate (LiNbO₃, LN) is the standard material for second-order () nonlinear optics. Frequency doubling, photon-pair sources, frequency converters and electro-optic modulators are all built from it. Almost everything about how it is used follows from one fact: the crystal has one special direction, the axis.

This note follows that axis through three questions.

  • Which polarizations of light mix, and how strongly? This is the d-matrix.
  • How is the crystal flipped to make periodically poled lithium niobate (PPLN)?
  • What changes when the chip is cut so that points out of the surface (z-cut) or lies in it (x-cut)?

The crystal: why z is special

Ions pushed off-center

LN is built from layers of oxygen stacked along . In the picture each layer is a triangle of three oxygen atoms, and two neighboring triangles close a cage. The metal ions sit on the axis in a fixed order along : lithium, niobium, empty cage. They do not sit at the symmetric positions (the dashed outlines). Each lithium ion is pushed a little out of its oxygen triangle, and each niobium ion a little off the center of its cage, all in the same direction along . Positive ions shifted against the negative oxygen frame give the crystal a built-in electric polarization, the spontaneous polarization , along .

Drag the picture to turn it. The shifts of the ions are drawn larger than they are.

Two jobs for one axis

  • Polar axis. points along or along , never in between. A region with one direction is called a domain. LN keeps its polarization up to about 1140 °C, so at room temperature a domain stays as it is until a strong electric field flips it.
  • Optic axis. Light polarized along sees the extraordinary index . Light polarized along or sees the ordinary index . Near 1300 nm, and .

The symmetry class of the crystal is 3m: a threefold rotation about and mirror planes that contain . Up and down along are different, so the crystal has no inversion symmetry. That is exactly what a response needs.

Why everyone wants

The conversion efficiency grows with the square of the coefficient in use, :

So the favorite arrangement is the bottom-right corner of the table: all three waves polarized along , coupled by .

The arrangements have names.

  • Type 0. All three waves have the same polarization. With , and this uses .
  • Type I. The two lower-frequency waves share a polarization and the highest-frequency wave is perpendicular to them. With and in and out this uses .
  • Type II. The two lower-frequency waves are perpendicular to each other. With and in and out this uses .

Type 0 has a price. When all waves have the same polarization, the two indices of the crystal cannot be used to keep the waves in step. The way out is to flip the crystal periodically, which is the next section.

Poling: flipping the crystal along z

A flipped domain has the opposite sign of d

Flipping a domain turns the crystal upside down along . The spontaneous polarization reverses, and with it the sign of every d coefficient:

To flip a domain, an electric field is applied along , against , stronger than the coercive field of the crystal (about 20 kV/mm in standard LN). Each lithium ion passes through the middle of its oxygen triangle into the empty cage next to it, the niobium ions shift, and the new direction stays when the field is removed. This is the motion in the picture above.

Doing this in stripes gives periodically poled lithium niobate: the sign of alternates along the waveguide with a period . How this keeps the waves in step, and how is chosen, belongs to the note on phase matching.

The rule to remember: the poling field has to point along . Where points on the chip decides where the electrodes go.

x-cut and z-cut

Which mode has its field along z?

To use , the electric field of the light has to point along . The cut decides which waveguide mode does that. A TE mode has its field in the plane of the chip, and a TM mode has its field perpendicular to it.

The electro-optic effect follows the same rule. Its largest coefficient needs both the field of the light and the applied field along .

On x-cut, direction matters

On a z-cut chip the TM field is along whichever way the waveguide runs, and every direction in the plane looks the same to the light. On an x-cut chip the TE field is along only when the waveguide runs along . If the waveguide is turned by an angle , the field makes the same angle with , and both the coefficient and the index change:

The sign of the last term in depends on which way the waveguide is turned.

Try it
0°90°

This is why straight PPLN waveguides on x-cut are laid out along , and why bends and rings on x-cut need care: around a bend the index changes by about 0.07, and the TE and TM modes can couple. On z-cut a ring looks the same all the way around.

Side by side

x-cutz-cut
Where pointsIn the plane of the chipOut of the chip
Mode that uses and TE, waveguide along TM, any direction
Poling electrodesTwo combs on the surface, one on each side of the waveguideFingers on top and a conductor below (the back face of a bulk crystal, a buried layer in a thin film)
Directions in the planeNot the same: the index runs from to All the same
Modulator electrodesOn the surface, beside the waveguideOn top of the waveguide, field through the film
Often used forThin-film PPLN waveguides, high-speed modulatorsBulk PPLN crystals, rings and bends, TM devices

Neither cut is better in general. Most thin-film PPLN waveguides and nearly all high-speed modulators are x-cut, because every electrode sits on the surface next to the waveguide. z-cut is the classic choice for bulk PPLN crystals. In thin films it is attractive when direction should not matter, or when the light is TM-polarized, as in the QFC chip on the Projects page, where a z-cut LN film is bonded on a silicon nitride strip.
